_comment: Company Brain realm, as configuration in the repository rather than as clicks in an
admin console. Task id M1.1.1.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS. A Keycloak realm configured by hand is a permission-adjacent
system whose current state nobody can diff, review or restore. Every value below is a
decision, and several of them are the difference between a working sign-in and a
silent bypass, so they belong where a reviewer sees them change.
IMPORTED AND VERIFIED on 2026-09-06 against Keycloak 26.0, which is what this file
had been waiting for. The earlier note here said it had never been imported and that
M1.1.1 could not be called done until it was. It has been now, so that note is gone
and this is what happened.
The import ran on a throwaway server, as the note asked: an ephemeral container bound
to localhost with a memory limit, never registered with Coolify, removed afterwards.
Keycloak reported 'Realm brain imported' and 'Import finished successfully'.
The first attempt logged three warnings and they were real: 'Referenced client scope
openid doesn't exist. Ignoring', and the same for profile and email. brain-console
listed all three and this file defines none of them, because a full import replaces
the client scope set with the one declared here. They are removed; see the note on
defaultClientScopes. The second import was silent.
What the server actually stored was then read back rather than assumed: RS256, the
ten-hour session, refresh revocation with no reuse, brute-force protection, no
password grant and no implicit flow on any client, PKCE S256 on the public one, and
the whole group tree including the scoped subgroups under approver and
department-admin. All of it matches what is written here.
One thing is still untested: ops/keycloak/setup.sh. The import above mounted this file
and started the server with --import-realm; it did not go through kcadm. The script's
own header says it has never been run and that remains true.
Realm JSON is version-sensitive. This was verified on 26.0; expect a different major
version to reject or ignore fields.
THE SETTINGS THAT MATTER, AND WHY:
defaultSignatureAlgorithm RS256, and every client pinned to it. brain.identity.oidc
refuses HS256 outright, because an HMAC-signed token is signed by anything holding the
client secret and the classic confusion attack presents the published RSA public key
as that secret. The two ends agree here so a misconfiguration fails at login rather
than becoming an accepted token.
ssoSessionMaxLifespan 36000 (10 hours) matches SESSION_ABSOLUTE_MAX in
brain.identity.sessions. If the realm allowed longer, a refresh loop would keep a
March sign-in alive in September on the Keycloak side while our own registry refused
it, and the mismatch would present as random logouts rather than as a policy.
revokeRefreshToken true with refreshTokenMaxReuse 0 makes a stolen refresh token
detectable: replaying one invalidates the chain. Without it a copied refresh token is
a ten-hour credential with no way to notice it was taken.
directAccessGrantsEnabled false everywhere. The password grant skips the browser flow,
which means it skips the second factor and every conditional step configured in it. A
flow whose checks can be bypassed by asking a different endpoint is not a flow.
implicitFlowEnabled false, standardFlowEnabled true, PKCE S256 required on the public
console client. The implicit flow puts the token in a URL fragment, which lands in
browser history and referrer headers.
GROUPS CARRY ROLES AND NEVER CAPABILITIES. The groups below map to the six platform
roles in brain.identity.roles through GroupRoleRule, and to nothing else. There is
deliberately no group, attribute or client role here that names a capability: putting
one in this file would move the answer to 'who can read the margin on this client'
into a directory that nobody in this company reviews.

groups.name: brain
groups._comment: A container, mapped to nothing. Membership of /brain alone confers no role.

subGroups.name: department-admin
_comment: Never mapped itself. department_admin is in SCOPE_REQUIRED, so a rule for it
must carry a scope, and only the per-department children below can supply one.
A rule for the bare parent would be a company-wide admin created by a group.

subGroups.name: approver
subGroups._comment: Also scope-required. Same rule as department-admin: children only.

clientScopes.name: brain-identity
clientScopes.description: The claims brain.identity.oidc.ClaimMapping reads. Nothing else.

config.claim.name: groups
config._comment: full.path true because GroupRoleRule compares the whole path exactly; a bare leaf name would make /brain/approver/web and /clientx/approver/web the same string.

clients.name: Company Brain console
clients.description: The browser app. Public client, authorisation code with PKCE.
_comment: brain-identity alone, and the three that used to sit beside it are gone.
This file previously listed openid, profile and email here. The first real import,
on 2026-09-06 against Keycloak 26.0, logged three warnings: 'Referenced client scope
openid doesn't exist. Ignoring', and the same for profile and email. They were
ignored because a full realm import replaces the client scope set with the one this
file declares, and this file declares only brain-identity. openid was wrong in a
second way as well: it is a scope value a client asks for in the request, never a
client scope an administrator defines.
Removing them changes no behaviour, because Keycloak was already discarding them.
What it changes is that the import is now silent, and an import that prints warnings
is one where the next person cannot tell the harmless lines from the real ones.
Nothing is lost. brain.identity.oidc reads exactly two claims, groups and department,
and brain-identity maps both. profile and email would add name and email claims that
nothing in this system consumes. When something does want them, they are added
deliberately, as a declared scope with its mappers, rather than as a name that
resolves to nothing.
webOrigins is an explicit origin and never '*' or '+'. A wildcard here lets any
site read a token from this realm.
backchannel.logout.session.required true makes Keycloak send the sid, which is
what SessionRegistry.end_session needs; end_all_for covers the case where it does
not arrive or the session was never seen by this replica.
redirectUris are .invalid placeholders on purpose. Setting a real hostname here
would put a production URL in a file that gets copied between environments, and a
stale redirect URI in a realm import is an open redirect.

clients.name: Company Brain API
clients.description: The audience every token this system accepts is minted for.

protocolMappers.name: brain-api-audience
protocolMappers._comment: Without an explicit audience mapper, a token minted for the console carries no aud for the API, and validate_token refuses it. That refusal is correct: a token is issued for a party, and accepting one issued for somebody else is the confused deputy.

clients.name: Example service account
clients.description: A machine caller. Client credentials only; no browser flow at all.
_comment: No secret is stored in this file and none ever should be. kcadm prints one on
creation; it belongs in OpenBao.
use.refresh.tokens false: a client-credentials caller can ask for a new token
whenever it likes, so a refresh token is a second long-lived credential with no
purpose.
This client's tokens carry no sid, which is how brain.identity.sessions keeps the
interactive and service paths disjoint. The owner, ceiling and expiry live in our
own ServiceAccount record, not here: Keycloak knows the robot exists, and this
system decides what it may borrow.
Template for M1.1.4, disabled and pointed at .invalid. A client's SAML IdP is added
per deployment; brain.identity.oidc.SamlFederation is the reviewed shape of these
same fields, and it refuses the two settings that are always got wrong:
wantAssertionsSigned false and validateSignature false, either of which turns an
assertion into a form post claiming to be a person.
principalType ATTRIBUTE with a stable attribute, never a transient NameID: a
transient identifier changes every session, so nobody would be recognised twice and
principal_for would return UnmappedSubject to the same person every morning.

requiredActions.name: Configure OTP
requiredActions._comment: defaultAction true so a new account is asked to set up a second factor at first login. Assurance.STRONG is what brain.gate.admission requires for approve and admin, so without this nobody can approve anything.
